title: Firewalls & Network Segmentation
summary: What a firewall actually filters, and how segmentation limits how far an attacker can move once one host is compromised.

slides.markdown:
A **firewall** is a chokepoint that decides which network traffic is allowed to pass, based on rules about addresses, ports, and protocols. It's the oldest network control in the book, and it's still on every architecture diagram.

But a firewall answers one question — *should this packet be let through* — and nothing else. It doesn't know if the allowed traffic is malicious, and it does nothing once traffic is already inside the network it protects.

That's where **segmentation** comes in: splitting the network into zones so that a compromise in one zone doesn't automatically hand over the rest. The two ideas are complementary, and interviewers care whether you can explain both — and where each one stops.

slides.subTitle: The five-tuple
slides.markdown:
A traditional firewall decides allow-or-drop using a small set of fields visible on every packet — commonly called the **five-tuple**: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, and protocol (TCP/UDP/ICMP).

A rule reads like: *allow TCP from any source to 10.0.1.5 on port 443, drop everything else destined for that host.* That's it — no awareness of what the request actually says.

**Connection state** adds one more dimension: a firewall can track whether a packet belongs to a connection that was legitimately opened, rather than judging each packet in isolation. That distinction — stateless vs. stateful — is the next slide, because it's the single biggest jump in what a firewall can enforce.

| | Stateless (packet filter) | Stateful (connection-tracking) |
|---|---|---|
| Decision basis | Each packet judged alone | Tracked per-connection state table |
| Return traffic | Needs its own explicit rule | Auto-allowed if it matches an open connection |
| Example gap | A rule allowing outbound port 80 must also separately allow the inbound reply | One rule: allow outbound; replies are implicitly permitted |
| Cost | Cheap, fast | Holds state per connection — a real memory/CPU cost at scale |

A stateless filter has to explicitly allow both halves of every conversation, which either over-permits (allow all high ports inbound, "just in case") or breaks legitimate traffic. A stateful firewall tracks the handshake and only allows a reply that actually matches an outbound request it saw — that single change closes off a huge amount of accidental exposure.

Almost every firewall you'll touch in production — cloud security groups, `iptables` with `conntrack`, enterprise NGFWs — is stateful by default. Pure stateless filtering survives mainly in access-control lists (ACLs) on routers.

A stateful firewall still only sees IPs, ports, and protocol — it can't tell HTTPS-carrying-a-file-upload from HTTPS-carrying-an-API-call, because both are "TCP port 443." A **next-generation firewall (NGFW)** inspects further up the stack: it identifies the actual application (Slack vs. a rogue app tunneling over port 443), decodes the protocol, and can apply rules like "allow HTTPS, but block file uploads over 50MB" or "allow Zoom, block BitTorrent even if it's disguised on port 443."

This is done through **deep packet inspection (DPI)** and signature/behavior matching, sometimes combined with decrypting TLS at the firewall to actually see payloads (with its own trust and privacy trade-offs).

The practical upshot: port-based rules alone are increasingly meaningless, because most traffic — legitimate and malicious — rides on port 443. Application awareness is what makes a modern firewall rule actually mean something.

slides.subTitle: Limiting blast radius
slides.markdown:
**Segmentation** splits a flat network into smaller zones with controlled paths between them, usually enforced with **VLANs** (logically separate broadcast domains on shared switching hardware) plus firewall rules or ACLs at the boundaries.

The motivating failure is a **flat network**: one compromised laptop can reach the database, the build server, and every other laptop, because nothing stood between them. Segmentation means that same laptop, if compromised, can only reach what its VLAN is explicitly allowed to reach.

This is the network-layer version of the **principle of least privilege**: a workload should only be reachable from — and able to reach — what it actually needs, nothing broader. Segmentation is what turns "one bad host" from "the whole network is compromised" into "one bad host, contained."

slides.subTitle: Isolating public-facing services
slides.markdown:
A **demilitarized zone (DMZ)** is a segment sitting between the public internet and the internal network, holding only the services that must be reachable from outside — a public web server, a mail relay, a reverse proxy.

The firewall rules are asymmetric on purpose: the internet can reach the DMZ on specific ports, the DMZ can reach specific internal services it genuinely needs (say, an app server on one port), and — critically — the internet can **never** reach the internal network directly, and the DMZ's access inward is as narrow as possible.

If the public web server in the DMZ is popped, the attacker lands in a zone with no database, no employee workstations, and no admin tooling — just whatever narrow path was granted inward, which should itself require authentication.

![A three-zone network diagram: internet reaches only the DMZ, the DMZ reaches one narrow port on an internal app server, and there is no direct internet-to-internal path](assets/dmz-network-zones.svg)

slides.markdown:
Every firewall ruleset should end with an implicit or explicit **default-deny**: if no rule matches, drop the packet. The alternative — default-allow, with a growing list of blocks — means every threat you haven't thought of yet is permitted by default. Default-deny inverts the burden: nothing gets through unless someone explicitly decided it should.

**Rule order matters** in most firewall engines: rules are evaluated top to bottom, and the first match wins. A broad `allow any` rule placed above a narrower `deny` rule silently makes that deny unreachable — a common, hard-to-spot misconfiguration during an audit.

A healthy ruleset is also **reviewed for drift**: temporary "just for this incident" rules that never got removed are one of the most common findings in a firewall audit, and they quietly erode the default-deny posture over months.

slides.subTitle: Why perimeter defense alone isn't enough
slides.markdown:
**North-south traffic** crosses the perimeter — internet to data center, or data center to internet. A traditional firewall at the edge is built for exactly this.

**East-west traffic** moves laterally inside the data center — service to service, host to host. Classic perimeter firewalls often sit blind to it entirely, because it never crosses the boundary they watch.

This gap is *why* attackers who breach one host care so much about lateral movement: once inside, east-west traffic is frequently unrestricted, so a single foothold can reach the database directly. Segmentation (and later, microsegmentation in zero-trust designs) exists specifically to put firewall-like controls **inside** the network, on east-west paths, not just at the edge.

An architecture with a hardened perimeter and a flat, trusting interior is a common real-world failure — most large breaches spread through east-west movement after an initial, unremarkable foothold.

A **network firewall** sits between network segments and filters traffic crossing that boundary — one device (or cloud construct) protecting many hosts. A **host-based firewall** runs on a single machine and filters traffic to and from that machine alone, regardless of which network segment it's on.

They're not substitutes. A network firewall can't stop two hosts *inside the same segment* from talking to each other — that's exactly the traffic it never sees. A host-based firewall (or its cloud equivalent, a **security group** attached to one instance) closes that gap by enforcing rules per-host, which is also what makes fine-grained microsegmentation possible without physically re-wiring the network.

In a cloud environment, this distinction maps directly onto **security groups** (host/instance-level, stateful) vs. **network ACLs** (subnet-level) — the same idea, implemented as software-defined policy instead of physical hardware.

slides.sectionTitle: Treating the firewall as the only control
slides.markdown:
The recurring mistake: budgeting all your network security effort into the perimeter firewall and assuming the interior is safe because the edge is guarded.

A firewall can't stop a phished employee's laptop from being the entry point — that traffic looks perfectly legitimate from outside. It can't stop a vulnerable internal service from being reached by another already-compromised internal host, because that's east-west traffic it may never see. And it does nothing once an attacker is running code with valid credentials inside the perimeter.

The fix is **defense in depth**: firewalls at the edge, segmentation inside, host-based controls on top of that, and identity checks that don't assume "inside the network" means "trusted" — the zero-trust model later in this group takes that idea all the way. A firewall is one layer among several, never the whole plan.
